Compression matters because recording, storage and communication all consume resources. The ITU reports 18.2 percent average annual growth in mobile broadband traffic since 2021. Its 2026 estimate is 1.7 zettabytes. These figures describe network traffic, not the entire amount of data created worldwide. LLMs and robots give intuitive examples of systems that handle multiple data types. The question becomes more delicate when the data are brain recordings.

These are the technique families in the website. Huffman coding and ZIP are general-purpose lossless ideas; PNG applies lossless coding to images. DEFLATE combines LZ77 string matching with Huffman coding. MP3 is perceptual audio coding, not an EEG compressor. Mu-law companding is invertible before quantization: the loss comes from subsequently using finitely many levels. PNG is lossless; JPEG is normally lossy. Thresholding and dithering can map grayscale to one bit per pixel; bit packing and file coding are still needed to store it compactly.

EEG is non-invasive scalp recording. Each channel measures voltage relative to another location or reference; it is not an isolated neuron's output or a direct reading of thoughts. Amplification, filtering and analog-to-digital conversion produce sampled multichannel time series. Scalp position and reference affect the measurements. Frequency content, changes across channels and responses aligned to stimuli provide different analysis features. Lossless predictors exploit repeated or predictable structure and encode what the predictor missed, without discarding sample values. Near-lossless coding permits bounded error. Transform-based lossy methods instead represent the waveform using coefficients and reduce their precision or discard some. Higgins studies quantization and thresholding within wavelet compression; our experiment uses a simpler DCT method, not their wavelet codec. Dao provides a survey and motivates compression ratio and waveform-distortion measures. Compression ratio is original bytes divided by stored bytes. PRD and NRMSE depend on the chosen normalization, so papers with different definitions or raw sample precision are not directly comparable. We do not put their compression ratios on a common performance leaderboard.

Preserving downstream recognition after compression is established work, not a novelty claim for this project. Zhang and colleagues combine DCT, personalized neural reconstruction and nonuniform quantization, and evaluate SSVEP recognition after reconstruction. Strypsteen and Bertrand jointly optimize source coding and an inference network for motor execution in an emulated wireless sensor network; this is not the same motor-imagery task used here. BrainCodec studies learned EEG/iEEG compression, including downstream and expert evaluations. Our narrower question asks how several simple compressors affect three tasks when the existing original-data reader remains frozen. We do not reproduce these neural codecs or claim to outperform them.

We chose three broad paradigms rather than several variants of one task. SSVEP identifies one of four visual flicker targets. Motor imagery distinguishes imagined left/right hand movements. P300 detects a target flash using the brief response after a stimulus; this is single-flash detection, not complete spelling accuracy. Different features may react differently to quantization or removal of frequency components. Comparing the same people and stored montage reduces confounds, while baseline difficulty and decoder design still differ.

Evaluation subjects are S07–S26, selected in advance. S03–S06 remain the separate pilot and S01–S02 are development checks. The input has the same twelve channels for every task. Continuous recordings are resampled to 128 Hz and filtered from 0.5 to 40 Hz. The split is chronological at 60 percent of events. Training epochs finish two seconds before the boundary, and test epochs begin two seconds after it. Filtering is offline and noncausal, which remains a limitation. SSVEP and MI epochs last four seconds; P300 epochs last one second. Overlapping P300 test epochs share a single encoded continuous recording. One-second codec frames choose the least waveform MSE among a predefined candidate grid that fits each cap, without labels or classifier outcomes. Models and event annotations are outside EEG payload for every method. Raw selected float32 requires 512 bytes/s/channel. Balanced accuracy averages recall across classes; chance is 25 percent for SSVEP and 50 percent for MI/P300. Each person's score receives equal weight. CCA uses known frequency templates. CSP is a learned spatial filter; LDA is linear discriminant analysis. Alternative readers are fixed in advance, calibrated on original early data and never adapted to compression. Both P300 readers share the same low-frequency time-bin features. A float32+ZIP control must recover exact samples and preserve predictions.

These are measured observations, not simulated curves. Lower loss is better; negative loss means a slightly higher reconstructed-data score. At the tightest cap the primary readers put SSVEP highest for every method. The alternative readers put P300 highest for uniform and mu-law, and SSVEP highest for DCT. The original baselines differ between readers, so this is sensitivity to the readout, not a contest to declare one universally better. Intervals are pointwise percentile intervals from participant-level resampling, not trial-level intervals or multiplicity-adjusted tests. Equal caps do not produce exactly equal achieved rates; those rates are exported on the site. Three primary motor-imagery baselines are weak and remain included. The four-person pilot's uniform and mu-law task ordering does not repeat in the larger primary cohort.

At 32 bytes/s/channel, primary mean losses are 12.13/9.22/9.47 pp for uniform, 12.95/10.91/9.60 for mu-law, and 8.82/4.10/0.61 for DCT, ordered SSVEP/MI/P300. All primary SSVEP-minus-MI paired intervals cross zero at this cap. SSVEP is the largest-loss task for only eight of twenty people under uniform, despite its largest group mean. Changing readers changes the task ordering. The strongest repeated local result is P300's DCT advantage over uniform: 8.87 pp with interval 7.95–9.83 for the primary reader, and 10.05 pp with interval 9.00–11.20 for the alternative. Every new participant shows that direction. Both P300 readers use the same low-frequency features, so this does not test all P300 analysis methods. P300 DCT changes about 5.9 percent of primary predictions despite only 0.61 pp mean score loss; correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct changes can partly cancel. Baseline difficulty matters: primary SSVEP still scores about 81 percent under tight-cap uniform while MI is about 61 percent against a 50 percent chance level.

The extension improves the sample size but still uses a fixed, nonrandom subset of one acquisition study. We have not tested a new day, real-time deployment, clinical interpretation or device power. The continuous noncausal filter can couple neighboring samples across the split despite the epoch guard. Original task difficulty differs, and weak baselines are retained. Each task has only two chosen readers. The alternative P300 reader changes the classifier but not the features, so a broader feature comparison is still needed. All codec settings were selected using waveform MSE, not task labels, but their search grids differ. Equal maximum byte caps leave different unused space. Future work should test more datasets and tasks, independently varied feature extractors, stronger EEG codecs and more closely matched achieved rates. Streaming and hardware experiments would be needed for latency or battery claims.
